subject: 측정은 무엇을 전제하는가
title: What every measurement quietly assumes
content: Measurement appears to be the plainest activity in the pursuit of knowledge. We apply an instrument, record a number, and treat the number as a piece of the world. Yet a philosophical argument shows that measuring assumes considerably more than it reports, and understanding those assumptions matters for judging what the resulting truth is worth. The first assumption concerns the quantity itself. Before anything can be measured, we must already believe that the property varies along a single dimension, so that one case genuinely holds more of it than another. Length satisfies this condition obviously. Intelligence, welfare, and creativity satisfy it far less obviously, therefore assigning them numbers may impose an order the property never possessed. The instrument carries a second assumption. Every device is calibrated against a standard, and the standard was itself established by a procedure somebody chose. Consequently a measurement reports a relation between the object and that shared convention rather than a bare fact. Although this does not make the number arbitrary, it does mean that the value depends upon a history of decisions, and those decisions embodied particular purposes. A third assumption concerns stability. We suppose that whatever we measure holds still long enough for the reading to apply, and that measuring does not disturb the thing measured. Both suppositions fail in familiar cases, since asking people about their attitudes can alter those attitudes, and observing very small systems changes them. The moral consequence is significant wherever numbers govern decisions. A quantity presented without its assumptions carries an authority it has not earned, and people defer to it precisely because it looks like a fact rather than a judgment. Publishing the procedure alongside the value restores the balance, because it lets others see which choices were made and contest them. Numbers remain among our best instruments for reaching truth, yet their value depends entirely upon whether we remember what producing them required.

subject: 기술 진보는 목표를 갖는가
title: Whether invention is heading anywhere
content: We speak of technical progress as though it were travelling toward somewhere. Machines become faster, smaller, and more capable, and the direction seems obvious enough that we rarely examine it. Yet a philosophical question hides inside the ordinary phrase. Progress implies an improvement measured against some purpose, therefore we must ask whose purpose is being served and whether it deserves the name. One answer holds that the purpose is internal to the enterprise. Each device solves a problem that earlier devices created or exposed, so the sequence has a logic of its own, and the direction requires no external justification. This account explains a great deal about how invention actually proceeds. It explains rather little, however, about why we should regard the sequence as valuable, since a chain of solutions can lead anywhere at all. A second answer supplies an external standard. Technical change counts as progress when it enlarges human freedom, reduces suffering, or extends the range of things people may reasonably choose. Although this standard has genuine moral content, applying it proves difficult, because almost every significant invention has done some of these things while undoing others. The same networks that carry knowledge across the world also carry deception across it. A third position denies that the sequence has any direction whatever. On this view what survives is whatever fits the interests of those able to fund it, and calling the outcome progress merely dresses a market result in moral language. The claim is uncomfortable, yet it explains why so much invention addresses the wants of the wealthy before the needs of the poor. What follows is not despair but attention. If direction is not automatic, then it must be chosen, argued about, and paid for, and the moral question about which inventions deserve support becomes a genuine public question rather than a technical detail left to whoever happens to be building.

subject: 기여가 미미할 때의 책임
title: Responsibility when your part is very small
content: Many serious harms are produced by enormous numbers of tiny contributions. No single vote decides an election, no single purchase sustains a cruel industry, and no single journey warms the atmosphere measurably. Consequently a person can survey their own conduct, find nothing that made a detectable difference, and conclude that they carry no moral responsibility whatever. The reasoning feels rigorous, and its conclusion is almost certainly false. One reply attacks the notion of a detectable difference. Detection is a fact about our instruments rather than about the world, therefore an effect too small to observe remains an effect. If a thousand people each add an imperceptible quantity of poison to a well, the well is poisoned, and every one of them contributed exactly what the poisoning consists of. Nothing in the argument permits the number of contributors to dissolve the harm. A second reply changes the moral question entirely. Rather than asking what my particular action accomplished, it asks what principle I could defend to everyone standing where I stand. The principle allowing each contributor to proceed because their share is negligible cannot be defended, since accepting it universally produces exactly the harm nobody wanted. Justice, on this reading, concerns the shareable reason rather than the measurable effect. A third reply notices what the original argument would license. If tiny contributions carried no responsibility, then organising a harm through many hands would be a method of committing it innocently, and that conclusion should be rejected on its face. Although none of these replies tells a person precisely how much they owe, together they establish that the answer is not nothing. What they recommend in practice is proportion rather than paralysis. A share of the responsibility is genuine but partial, and the reasonable response is to reduce one's contribution where doing so is possible while supporting the arrangements that reduce everybody's at once.

subject: 능력주의의 도덕적 한계
title: How far merit can carry a claim
content: Rewarding people according to merit appears to be the fairest rule we have. Positions go to whoever performs best, and nobody is excluded by birth, so the principle looks like justice itself. Yet the moral argument supporting it is much weaker than its popularity suggests, and examining that argument reveals several genuine limits. The first limit concerns the origin of ability. Talent arrives through inheritance and early circumstance, neither of which anybody selected, and the willingness to work hard depends heavily upon an upbringing that encouraged it. Therefore the qualities that merit rewards are themselves substantially unearned, and a principle rewarding unearned qualities cannot claim the moral authority that desert would supply. A second limit concerns what counts as merit. Every selection measures certain abilities, and the choice of which abilities to measure reflects the values of whoever designed the test. A society valuing speed will find different people meritorious than one valuing patience, although neither ranking discovers a truth about human worth. Therefore merit is less a natural standard than a decision presented as a discovery. A third limit concerns the effect upon those who lose. Where positions are distributed by birth, the excluded may resent the system while retaining their self respect. Where positions are distributed by measured merit, the same people are invited to conclude that the outcome reflects what they are, and that conclusion corrodes something a decent society should protect. Although these limits are serious, they do not establish that merit should be abandoned. Selecting surgeons by ability rather than by family remains obviously right, because the point is competence rather than desert. What the limits establish is that merit justifies a certain assignment of tasks without justifying the vast rewards attached to them, and that separating those two questions is the beginning of a more honest argument about justice.

subject: 사랑은 이유를 갖는가
title: Whether love answers to reasons
content: Ask somebody why they love another person and the answers arrive readily. They are kind, they are funny, they understand me. Yet a philosophical difficulty appears immediately, because such answers seem to describe qualities rather than the person, and qualities can be found elsewhere. If I love somebody for their kindness, then apparently I should transfer my affection to whoever proves kinder, and the suggestion strikes almost everybody as monstrous. One response abandons reasons entirely. Love, on this view, fastens upon a particular person rather than upon a description, therefore asking for justification misunderstands the relation. The account captures something true about how love actually behaves, since we do not ordinarily audit our attachments against alternatives. It captures rather little, however, about the difference between love and mere fixation, and that difference clearly matters morally. A second response keeps the reasons while changing their function. The qualities we name do not justify the attachment in the way evidence justifies a belief; instead they explain how it began and what sustains it. Consequently a superior candidate poses no threat, because the reasons were never competing entries in a ranking. Although this reading is more plausible, it leaves open what happens when the qualities disappear entirely. A third position emphasises history. What we love is not a collection of traits but a person known over time, and the knowledge accumulated within a shared life cannot be replicated by any newcomer, however admirable. On this account love has reasons of a peculiar sort: reasons that could not apply to anybody else, because nobody else has that history. The moral value of this picture lies in what it demands. It makes love something built rather than merely found, and it explains why the virtue involved is constancy rather than accurate judgment, since the relation is sustained by attention rather than by continual reassessment of the evidence.

subject: 진정성이라는 이상
title: The ideal of being genuinely oneself
content: Modern moral language places extraordinary weight upon being true to oneself. We praise authenticity, we criticise pretence, and we advise the young to follow whatever they genuinely are rather than whatever others expect. The ideal feels obviously correct, yet its philosophical foundations are unclear, and examining them exposes both a genuine value and a familiar confusion. The confusion lies in supposing that a self exists beforehand, waiting to be discovered and expressed. On that picture authenticity requires only accurate reporting, and any external demand counts as distortion. But people are formed by languages, families, and traditions they never selected, therefore stripping away those influences would not reveal an inner person; it would leave nothing at all. Whatever a self is, it was made rather than found. A better reading treats authenticity as a relation between a person and their own commitments. Somebody lives authentically when the values guiding their conduct are ones they have examined and endorsed, rather than ones absorbed without notice. Consequently the ideal demands reflection rather than isolation, and it remains entirely compatible with owing a great deal to other people. Although this version is less romantic, it preserves what the ideal was defending. There is a real moral difference between a life shaped by considered commitments and a life shaped by drift, and that difference shows in how a person behaves under pressure. The examined commitment holds; the absorbed one collapses whenever the surrounding expectations change. A final caution concerns how the ideal is used. Appeals to authenticity can excuse whatever somebody feels like doing, as though a strong impulse carried moral authority merely by being one's own. Nothing in the argument supports that conclusion. Being genuinely oneself is a virtue about the relation between a person and their values, and it settles nothing whatever about whether those values are good.

subject: 유비 추론의 힘과 한계
title: Reasoning from one case to another
content: Arguing by analogy is among the oldest instruments of moral thought. We compare an unfamiliar case with a familiar one, observe that the two resemble each other in relevant respects, and conclude that whatever holds in the first should hold in the second. Courts reason this way constantly, and so does anybody defending a moral position through examples. The strength of such reasoning lies in what it does not require. We need not possess a general principle covering every case; we need only judge that two situations are alike in whatever respects actually matter. Consequently analogy allows careful thinking in territory where no adequate theory exists, and moral life supplies a great deal of such territory. The weakness lies in exactly the same place. Any two situations resemble each other in countless respects and differ in countless others, therefore the argument depends entirely upon which similarities are held to be relevant. That judgment is not itself delivered by the analogy, and disputes about it cannot be settled by piling up further resemblances. Although a well chosen comparison can shift somebody's view immediately, a badly chosen one can smuggle a conclusion past their attention. This explains a familiar experience in argument. Somebody offers a comparison, the other person accepts it, and only afterwards do they notice that the accepted case differed in precisely the respect at issue. The remedy is to state the relevant similarity openly rather than leaving it implicit, since a stated principle can be examined whereas an implied one cannot. What emerges is a picture of analogy as a genuine but partial instrument. It proposes a conclusion and shifts the burden of argument onto whoever would reject the comparison. It does not establish truth by itself, and treating it as though it did is among the commonest failures in public moral reasoning.

subject: 아동의 권리와 부모의 권위
title: The child, the parent, and the claim between them
content: Parents exercise extensive authority over people who never consented to it. They decide where a child lives, what they learn, which beliefs surround them, and what medical treatment they receive. In any other relation such control would require serious justification, therefore the moral question is what makes this arrangement legitimate rather than merely traditional. One familiar answer appeals to capacity. Children cannot yet judge their own interests reliably, so somebody must judge for them, and parents are ordinarily best placed to do it. The argument has genuine force, although it establishes less than parents sometimes assume. It justifies authority exercised for the child, not authority exercised over the child for the parent's benefit, and it shrinks steadily as capacity develops. A second consideration concerns the child's future freedom. Because a child will become an adult with values of their own, decisions taken now shape somebody who does not yet exist to object. This suggests a moral constraint that is easily overlooked: upbringing should leave the eventual adult able to reconsider whatever they were given. An education that forecloses every alternative has taken something from a person who could not defend it. Yet the opposite extreme is incoherent. Nobody can raise a child without transmitting particular values, a particular language, and particular attachments, since a childhood emptied of commitments would leave the adult with nothing to reconsider. Therefore the constraint cannot demand neutrality; it can only demand that the door remain open. What follows is a picture of parental authority as genuine but held in trust. Parents hold it because somebody must, they exercise it toward the interests of a person who cannot yet speak, and they surrender it gradually rather than at a single moment. Understanding the relation this way explains why the ordinary conflicts of adolescence are not merely friction but the visible transfer of a right.

subject: 위험 인식의 합리성
title: When fear tracks something real
content: People fear rare events and tolerate common ones, and this pattern is frequently described as an error. Statistics show that ordinary journeys kill far more people than dramatic accidents, therefore the public is said to misjudge danger, and experts are urged to correct it. Yet the moral philosophy underlying this verdict deserves examination, because judging risk involves values as well as arithmetic. Consider what a number reports. An expected quantity of harm combines how likely an outcome is with how bad it would be, and it treats those two components as exchangeable. But people care about features the product ignores entirely. They care whether the harm arrives all at once or spread thinly, whether they accepted the risk or had it imposed, and whether the loss could be recovered from. These concerns are not confusions about probability; they are judgments about value. A community may reasonably decide that a single catastrophe destroying one town is worse than the same total harm distributed across a decade, because concentrated losses destroy things that scattered ones do not. Similarly a risk somebody chose stands on different moral ground than one arranged for them by others who gain from it. Consequently the charge of irrationality frequently mistakes a disagreement about values for an error about facts. This does not mean every public fear is justified. People genuinely do misjudge frequencies, particularly when vivid examples are available, and correcting those misjudgments is worthwhile. The point is narrower and more important: once the frequencies are agreed, questions remain that no calculation settles, and those questions belong to everybody rather than to experts alone. The practical lesson concerns how such arguments should be conducted. Presenting a number as though it ended the discussion conceals the values embedded in constructing it, and that concealment does more damage to public trust than any disagreement about the number itself.

subject: 상속은 정당화되는가
title: Passing wealth to those who follow
content: Inheritance sits awkwardly within almost every theory of justice. Property is ordinarily defended by appeal to what somebody earned, produced, or freely exchanged, yet an inheritance arrives through none of these routes. The recipient did nothing whatever, and the resulting advantage compounds across generations, therefore the practice appears to violate the very principles that justify holding property at all. One defence shifts attention from the recipient to the giver. Whatever a person may rightfully hold, they may rightfully transfer, and forbidding a parent to provide for a child restricts the freedom of somebody who earned the wealth rather than the one receiving it. This argument has genuine moral force, since the alternative permits the state to seize whatever a person spent a lifetime accumulating precisely when they can no longer use it. A second defence appeals to the family. Providing for one's children expresses an attachment that most moral traditions treat as valuable, and a rule preventing it would strike at something deeper than economic advantage. Although this consideration is real, it justifies far less than unlimited transfer, because the attachment is expressed adequately by ordinary provision rather than by dynastic accumulation. The objection remains powerful nonetheless. Large inheritance produces exactly what merit was supposed to abolish, namely position determined by birth, and it does so while the surrounding society continues to describe outcomes as earned. That combination is corrosive, since it teaches people that unequal results reflect unequal effort when frequently they reflect unequal ancestors. What emerges is a case for limitation rather than abolition. Modest transfer honours both the giver's freedom and the family attachment, whereas very large transfer serves neither purpose while undermining the moral foundation of property itself. Where exactly the line should fall is a question about values rather than arithmetic, but the argument establishes that some line belongs there.

subject: 겸손은 덕인가
title: Whether thinking less of oneself is good
content: Humility appears on almost every traditional list of virtues, and yet its moral credentials are surprisingly hard to establish. If humility means underrating one's own abilities, then it requires a false belief, and no virtue should demand that somebody be wrong about themselves. If instead it means merely declining to boast, then it seems a matter of manners rather than character. Neither reading supports the weight the tradition places upon it. A better account locates the virtue elsewhere. Humility, on this reading, concerns attention rather than self assessment. The humble person is not preoccupied with their own standing, therefore they can attend to the work, the argument, or the other person without constantly measuring how they appear. Somebody may know perfectly well that they are the ablest person present and still possess this virtue, provided the knowledge does not organise their attention. This explains several things the earlier readings could not. It explains why humility and genuine confidence coexist so comfortably, since both involve being untroubled about one's position. It explains why the anxious person who constantly disparages their own work is not humble but merely preoccupied from the opposite direction. And it explains why humility improves the pursuit of truth, because somebody unconcerned with appearing right can change their view when the evidence demands it. The moral value follows directly. A person free from continual self assessment listens better, learns faster, and treats others as participants rather than as an audience. These are not small goods, and they are unavailable to anybody whose attention returns constantly to their own standing. Understood this way, humility is neither self deception nor mere modesty of speech. It is a particular freedom, and like most freedoms it is easier to admire than to acquire, since the habit of watching oneself is among the hardest things any person ever manages to set down.

subject: 서사적 통일성과 좋은 삶
title: Whether a life should hold together like a story
content: Some philosophers argue that a good life possesses the shape of a story. Its parts connect, earlier choices explain later ones, and the whole can be understood as a single unfolding rather than as a sequence of unrelated episodes. On this view the moral question is not merely whether certain actions were right, but whether the life they compose makes sense. The argument has wide appeal. Human beings do understand themselves through narrative, since explaining who we are involves saying where we came from and what we are trying to do. Commitments extend across years, therefore a life without continuity would make promises, friendships, and long projects impossible. Therefore narrative unity looks less like an optional aesthetic preference than like a condition of certain genuine values. Yet the ideal faces a serious objection. Many lives are broken by circumstances nobody chose, and demanding that they cohere adds an insult to whatever the person already suffered. Illness, exile, and poverty interrupt the projects through which unity was supposed to be achieved, and telling those affected that their lives lack shape imposes a further burden. A second objection concerns honesty. Stories are constructed afterwards, and constructing one means selecting whatever fits while quietly discarding the rest. Someone committed to a narrative about themselves may therefore misread their own past, treating accidents as decisions and luck as merit. The value of truth argues against too much attachment to the shape. A moderate position preserves the insight without the demand. Continuity of commitment is truly valuable, because it makes possible the goods that require time. Complete unity is neither achievable nor needed, and a life containing loose episodes, abandoned attempts, and unexplained turns may be wholly good. What matters morally is whether the person kept faith with whatever they undertook, not whether the whole reads well when told.

subject: 색채 이름과 그것이 나눈 스펙트럼
title: How cultures cut the rainbow into names
content: The visible spectrum arrives as a continuous band, yet no culture treats it that way. Every tradition divides the range into a modest set of named categories, and the divisions differ widely from one language to another. Some cultures name five basic colours, others eleven, and the boundaries fall at different places, therefore the same painted surface may belong to different categories depending upon who describes it. This variation once suggested that colour naming was wholly arbitrary. Careful comparison across many cultures overturned that conclusion. The names appear in a strikingly regular order, since traditions with only a few terms invariably distinguish dark from light, then add a term covering red, and only afterwards separate green, yellow, and blue. Therefore the cultural design is neither arbitrary nor identical everywhere, but built upon a shared foundation in perception. The artistic consequences run deep. A painter working within a tradition that treats green and blue as one category will handle those pigments differently from one whose language separates them, because the names on hand shape which contrasts appear worth marking. Textile traditions show this clearly, since the colours a culture names are usually the colours it learns to produce reliably in dye. Although the pigments to hand also constrain the naming, the influence runs in both directions. Literature offers a further illustration. Ancient poetry often describes the sea and honey with the same term, and readers have long puzzled over the apparent confusion. The poets were not colour blind; their vocabulary simply marked brightness and texture where later languages mark hue. Understanding this transforms passages that once seemed merely strange into precise descriptions using a different scheme. What the whole case shows is how a cultural instrument shapes an aesthetic tradition without determining it. Names direct attention, attention shapes practice, and practice eventually makes the works through which a culture teaches its members what to see.

subject: 문학 장르는 어떻게 굳는가
title: How a kind of book becomes a category
content: Literary genres feel permanent to readers who inherit them. A novel of detection, a tragedy, or a romance seems to possess an obvious shape, and departures from that shape register immediately as departures. Yet every such category was assembled historically, and tracing the assembly reveals how cultural conventions harden into something resembling natural kinds. The process ordinarily begins with a successful work rather than a rule. One novel or play attracts imitation, the imitations share whatever features appeared responsible for the success, and gradually a cluster of expectations forms around them. Consequently the genre exists as a pattern in the audience before anybody states it, and early practitioners are frequently unaware of belonging to a category at all. Publishing and criticism then complete the work. Booksellers require shelves, reviewers require comparisons, and both need names, therefore the loose cluster acquires a label. Once labelled, the category begins to act upon writers rather than merely describing them. An author now knows what a detective story owes its reader, and satisfying or defeating that expectation becomes part of the artistic material. This explains why genres tighten over time and then break. Each generation of writers works within the inherited shape until its conventions become so visible that following them appears mechanical. The most interesting works of a mature genre are ordinarily those that expose its machinery, and such works simultaneously extend the tradition and begin dismantling it. Although readers frequently treat genre as a limitation upon creative freedom, the relation is considerably more useful than that. A shared form supplies expectations that an artist may satisfy, delay, or overturn, and none of those effects would be available without it. The category is not a cage but an instrument, and like other cultural instruments it works precisely because the audience learned it long before anybody explained what they had learned.

subject: 음식의 조리법과 문화 경계
title: What a recipe records besides ingredients
content: A recipe looks like a technical document, listing materials and operations needed to produce a dish. Yet recipes preserve a great deal that has nothing to do with technique, and reading them attentively reveals how a culture organised its daily life. In this respect a cookbook belongs alongside other artistic records of a tradition. Consider what the instructions assume. A method calling for continuous stirring assumes someone free to stir, therefore it belongs to a household with labour to spare or to a professional kitchen. A method requiring long unattended cooking assumes a hearth that stayed warm anyway, which locates the dish within a certain architecture. Therefore the technique encodes a way of living rather than merely a way of cooking. Ingredients record boundaries just as clearly. Traditions often treat certain combinations as unthinkable while allowing others that outsiders find strange, and these rules rarely follow from taste alone. They follow from ritual differences, from religious classification, and from the long habit of a region. Although newcomers experience such rules as arbitrary, insiders experience them as obvious, which is the ordinary signature of a cultural pattern rather than a practical one. Migration reveals the design most clearly. When a cuisine travels, the ingredients change first because supply changes, whereas the structure of a meal changes last. A community may substitute nearly every material and still preserve the sequence of courses, the shape of the shared plate, and the occasions on which certain dishes appear. That persistence shows which elements carried the cultural weight. What follows is a way of reading these documents as tradition rather than as instruction. A recipe transmits the aesthetic judgments of a community about balance, richness, and the proper end of a meal, and those judgments survive translation into new materials far better than any single ingredient ever does.

subject: 영화 편집이 만드는 인과
title: How a cut persuades us that one thing caused another
content: Film assembles its meaning from fragments recorded separately, and the audience experiences the result as continuous. This achievement depends upon editing, and the art of editing rests upon a peculiarity of perception that early filmmakers discovered by experiment rather than by theory. Place a neutral face beside an image of food and viewers report hunger; place the identical face beside a coffin and they report grief. Nothing in the performance changed. The audience supplied a relation between the two images, and the supplied relation felt like something they observed rather than something they contributed. Consequently the cut became the medium's most powerful instrument, since it constructs causes and feelings out of mere adjacency. Continuity editing developed as a set of conventions exploiting this tendency. Matching the direction of a glance, preserving screen position across a cut, and beginning a movement in one shot while completing it in the next all persuade viewers that separate fragments belong to a single space. Although none of these devices imitates ordinary vision, audiences learned them so thoroughly that violations register as errors rather than as style. Other traditions pursued the opposite possibility. Filmmakers who wished the audience to notice the construction cut against continuity deliberately, breaking spatial logic so that viewers would attend to the argument rather than sink into the illusion. This choice is aesthetic rather than technical, and it distinguishes whole schools of cinema from one another. What the history demonstrates is that a medium's grammar is invented rather than given. Nothing about photographed images required that adjacency should imply causation, yet once the convention was established it became the foundation of an art form. Every viewer who follows a film without effort has absorbed an elaborate cultural training, and the invisibility of that training is exactly the measure of how completely the convention succeeded.

subject: 악기의 개량과 음색의 변화
title: When an instrument changes, the music changes
content: Musical instruments are often treated as neutral vehicles for whatever a composer imagines. The history of their construction suggests the opposite relation, since improvements in design have repeatedly altered what music could sound like and therefore what composers thought to write. Consider the keyboard. Early instruments plucked their strings, making a bright tone that could not be made louder or softer by touch. Replacing the pluck with a hammer allowed the player to control volume through the fingers, and that single change made possible an entire aesthetic of gradual swelling and sudden emphasis. Composers did not merely adopt the new instrument; they began imagining musical gestures that the earlier design could not have carried. Wind instruments tell a similar story. Adding keys allowed notes outside the natural series to be played reliably and in tune, therefore melodies could travel through distant keys without the awkward tone that previously marked such passages. What had been a technical limitation had shaped the aesthetic rules of an entire tradition, and removing the limitation dissolved the rules along with it. The relation runs in both directions, however. Instrument makers responded to demands that performers and composers already felt, so the design changes record artistic ambitions as much as they cause them. A tradition wanting greater volume in larger halls pressed for heavier strings and stronger frames, and the resulting instruments then made a sound that later listeners came to regard as the natural sound of the music. This creates a real problem for players today. Playing older music on modern instruments makes a tone the composer never heard, whereas playing it on rebuilt instruments makes one that modern audiences find thin. Neither choice is simply correct, and the argument between them is an aesthetic argument about what a musical work actually is rather than a technical dispute about equipment.

subject: 무대 조명이 바꾼 연기
title: What electric light did to acting
content: Theatre spent most of its history in daylight or candlelight, and both conditions shaped performance in ways that are easy to overlook. Outdoor playhouses lit by the sun placed the audience and the performers within a single illuminated space, therefore the actors could see the crowd and address it directly. Candlelit indoor stages were dim, unsteady, and required the performer to remain near the light source. Under such conditions acting was necessarily broad. Gesture had to carry across distance without much help from the face, and the voice bore most of the interpretive weight. The style that resulted was not a failure of subtlety but an adaptation to what the audience could actually perceive, and the surviving plays were written for exactly those capacities. Controllable lighting altered every one of these conditions. A darkened house separated the audience from the stage, converting spectators into observers of a lit world rather than participants sharing a room. The performer could now be seen in detail, so the small movement of an eye became legible to people seated far away, and an entire aesthetic of restraint became available. Consequently the art of acting reorganised itself around the face. Playwriting followed. Scenes could begin in the middle of an action because light could reveal a situation instantly, and locations could change without spoken explanation because the design carried the information. The tradition of announcing time and place within the dialogue, which earlier drama required, gradually disappeared from the craft. Although these changes are usually described as technical progress, they were equally losses. Something valuable vanished when the audience stopped being visible to the performers, since the shared room had made theatre a public event rather than a private one witnessed collectively. Modern companies that light the audience deliberately are recovering a possibility the technology made easy to forget.

subject: 서예와 필적의 미학
title: The written stroke as an art of its own
content: In several traditions the written character is treated as a major art rather than as a vehicle for language. This judgment can puzzle observers whose culture regards handwriting as merely functional, yet the aesthetic reasoning behind it is coherent and worth understanding. The stroke records a movement. Because the brush responds to pressure, speed, and angle, the finished mark preserves the gesture that produced it, and a trained viewer can read that gesture as clearly as a listener hears phrasing in music. Consequently the work is valued not only for its final shape but for the visible history of its making, which cannot be revised afterwards without the correction showing. This explains why the tradition prizes qualities that seem paradoxical to outsiders. A slightly dry stroke, where the brush was running short of ink, is admired rather than concealed, since it demonstrates the speed of the hand. Irregularity is valued where it arises from momentum and criticised where it arises from hesitation, therefore the judgment concerns the movement rather than the resulting outline. The relation to meaning is subtle. The characters ordinarily say something, and what they say matters, yet the aesthetic judgment operates largely independently of the text. A famous work may record an ordinary letter or a draft with visible corrections, and the corrections themselves become part of what viewers admire, because they show a mind working. Although Western tradition developed elaborate calligraphy as well, it generally attached the art to decoration and to the sacred rather than treating the individual hand as an expressive subject. The difference is instructive. It shows that whether a practice counts as art depends less upon the materials than upon whether a culture develops the vocabulary, the connoisseurship, and the accumulated comparisons that make fine distinctions visible to those trained within it.

subject: 건축 재료의 지역성
title: Why buildings once looked like their ground
content: Before materials travelled cheaply, architecture was made from whatever lay nearby, and that constraint produced the regional styles later generations came to admire as tradition. Stone districts built in stone, timber districts in timber, and clay districts in brick, therefore the appearance of a settlement recorded its geology as directly as any map. The constraint shaped far more than surface appearance. Each material carries structural possibilities and refusals, so the available substance determined how wide a room could span, how tall a wall could stand, and where openings could be cut. A timber tradition develops framing and joinery, whereas a stone tradition develops the arch and the buttress, and the resulting interiors feel different in ways that have nothing to do with decoration. Climate reinforced these patterns. Thick masonry suits a region with hot days and cold nights because it stores warmth, while raised timber construction suits a wet region because it sheds water and permits air to move underneath. Consequently the local style was rarely arbitrary; it encoded generations of accumulated judgment about what actually worked in that place. Cheap transport dissolved the constraint. A builder anywhere may now specify materials from any source, and the same design can be erected in entirely different climates. This freedom produced genuine artistic gains, since architects were released from limitations that had nothing to do with what a building was for. It also produced a familiar loss, because settlements everywhere began resembling one another. Contemporary practice has partly returned to the older logic, though for different reasons. Transporting heavy materials consumes considerable energy, and buildings designed against their climate consume more, therefore local substance and local form have recovered a practical justification. What began as necessity, became tradition, and then became a style choice, is now becoming necessity again in an unexpected form.

subject: 연극의 제4의 벽과 관객의 자리
title: The invisible wall and where it puts the audience
content: Much modern theatre is performed as though an invisible wall stood between the stage and the seats. The characters behave as if unobserved, the audience watches a room from which it is absent, and the convention feels so natural that many spectators never notice it exists. Yet this arrangement is a comparatively recent cultural invention, and earlier traditions worked entirely differently. Older drama frequently addressed the audience directly. Characters explained their intentions aloud, commented upon the action, and appealed to the crowd for judgment, therefore the spectators were participants in a shared occasion rather than observers of a sealed world. The design suited playhouses where everybody stood in the same light and the performance competed with the noise of the street. The sealed room arrived alongside darkened auditoriums and a new ambition for illusion. Once the audience could no longer be seen, addressing it became awkward, and the aesthetic goal shifted toward persuading spectators that they were witnessing life rather than art. Consequently acting became more restrained, staging became more detailed, and any acknowledgement of the crowd registered as a break in the fabric. Twentieth century theatre discovered that the break itself could be an instrument. Deliberately puncturing the wall interrupts absorption and returns spectators to their own judgment, which is precisely what a playwright wants when the aim is argument rather than sympathy. The device works only because the convention is strong; without a wall there is nothing to break. What the history reveals is that the audience's position is an artistic choice rather than a fact about theatre. A tradition may place spectators inside the occasion or outside the frame, and each arrangement supports different kinds of work. Neither is more natural, although whichever a culture inherits will always feel that way to those who grew up within it.

subject: 문신과 신체 장식의 문화적 문법
title: Marks on the body and what they say
content: Permanent marking of the body appears in nearly every human tradition, and the practices differ so widely that no single explanation covers them. Yet the variation is not random, since these marks almost always function as a language, and reading them requires knowing the grammar of the culture that produced them. In many traditions the design records position. A particular pattern marks somebody who has completed an initiation, borne a child, or taken a role within the community, therefore the body carries information that would otherwise require introduction. Because the mark is permanent, it makes a claim that cannot be casually withdrawn, and that permanence is precisely what gives it authority. Other traditions use the practice to mark belonging rather than achievement. Shared designs identify a lineage or a region, and the aesthetic details differ enough between neighbouring groups that an informed observer can place a stranger immediately. Consequently the art form carries the same cultural work that dress and dialect perform elsewhere, with the difference that it cannot be exchanged when convenient. Modern practice has largely detached the mark from these functions. Contemporary designs ordinarily express individual taste, commemorate private attachments, or simply pursue beauty, and the meaning is available only to whoever chooses to explain it. Although this looks like a loss of grammar, a new one has formed, since styles cluster into recognisable schools and practitioners are judged by other practitioners against demanding standards. What persists across all these traditions is the peculiar power of using the body as the surface. A painting may be sold and a garment removed, whereas this art remains attached to the person who carries it and ages along with them. That inseparability is the source of both the seriousness such marks have carried in traditional cultures and the ambivalence they still provoke in societies that treat the body as private.

subject: 전통 악기의 조율 체계 차이
title: Why the notes themselves differ between traditions
content: Listeners often assume that music everywhere uses the same notes, arranged differently. The assumption is mistaken, since traditions divide the octave in truly different ways, and those divisions shape what the music can express as deeply as any choice of melody or rhythm. A tuning system solves a problem that has no perfect solution. The intervals that sound most consonant cannot all be fitted into a fixed set of pitches simultaneously, therefore every system accepts some compromise, and different traditions accept different ones. The compromise chosen fixes which harmonies sound pure, which sound strained, and which are missing altogether. European practice eventually adopted a division into twelve equal steps. This system makes every key sound alike, which lets music travel freely between them, and an enormous aesthetic tradition was built upon that option. The cost is that no interval except the octave is exactly in tune, so the characteristic colour that single keys once possessed disappeared along with the older systems. Other traditions made different bargains. Several use intervals smaller than any found in European practice, and their melodic art depends upon contrasts that a keyboard cannot produce. Instruments in those traditions are built accordingly, therefore a piano cannot play the music at all rather than merely playing it badly. Ensembles elsewhere tune to a scale whose steps are nearly equal but not identical, making a shimmer between instruments that is deliberate rather than accidental. Understanding this changes how one hears unfamiliar music. Passages that initially seem out of tune are often exactly in tune within their own system, and the strangeness is a report about the listener's training rather than about the playing. What sounds natural in any tradition is the system its members absorbed before they could describe it, which is the ordinary condition of every aesthetic rule.

subject: 복원과 위조 사이의 경계
title: Restoring a work without inventing it
content: Every old painting reaching a modern gallery has been treated, and the treatment raises a question that conservation cannot avoid. Cleaning removes later varnish and repaint, filling repairs losses, and retouching disguises the repairs, therefore what the visitor sees is partly the work of people who died centuries after the artist. Where restoration ends and invention begins is genuinely difficult to say. The difficulty is sharpest where information is missing. A damaged area may be filled with neutral tone, which is honest but interrupts the design, or it may be reconstructed from what surrounds it, which restores the aesthetic experience while asserting something nobody actually knows. Both choices are defensible, and both alter what the audience believes it is seeing. Modern practice attempts a compromise through reversibility and visibility. Materials are chosen so that later conservators can undo the work, and retouching is applied in fine lines or slightly different tone so that close inspection reveals it while ordinary viewing does not. Consequently the tradition tries to serve two audiences simultaneously, the visitor who wants the picture and the scholar who wants the evidence. Forgery inverts every one of these commitments. The forger also imitates an earlier style with great skill, but conceals the intervention rather than recording it, and claims a history the object does not possess. The technical operations may be nearly identical while the moral relation is opposite, which shows that the boundary lies in disclosure rather than in craft. This explains why documentation matters so much within the field. A restored painting accompanied by a full account of what was done remains an honest object, whereas the same painting without that account becomes a claim nobody can check. The art of conservation therefore consists as much in keeping records as in handling materials, since the record is what separates the two practices.
